solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Made many of crowd push, engulfing Mussolini

parts.note: a mass is a large crowd of people

indicators.note: to engulf is to swallow up whole, so one word wraps itself around the other

parts.note: to prod is to push or poke
Il Duce, 'the leader', was Mussolini's title

explanation.surface: A dictator is caught up in a pushing crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Il Duce, Italian for 'the leader', was the title Mussolini took as Fascist dictator.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods turned out in huge numbers on a factory line are said to be mass-produced, the verb's past form matching 'made'.

clue.text: Picasso initially divides a painting into sections

indicators.note: dividing something means getting in between its parts, so one piece sits inside the other
initially points to the opening letter of the painter's name only

explanation.surface: Picasso's cubism is described as chopping a picture into fragments.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taken apart is broken into separate pieces, so the adverb fits 'into sections' as in 'take it apart'.

clue.text: Like those made homeless, unexpectedly in the main

definitions.text: Like those made homeless, unexpectedly in the main

parts.note: surface reading: people suddenly evicted from their homes
setter's reading: the main is the open sea, so these people lost their vessel at sea

explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' looks like 'mostly', but in old poetic usage the main is the ocean; sailors whose vessel sinks are left with nowhere to live.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors cast adrift after their vessel sinks at sea have lost their floating home, which is exactly this adjective's sense.

clue.text: Girl with net twisted around curly hair

indicators.note: twisted around suggests letters bent out of their original order into a new shape

explanation.surface: A girl wears a hairnet over her curls.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringlet is a single lock of hair hanging in a spiral curl, as a noun phrase matches.

clue.text: Guy in Washington, mostly useless

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: dude is American slang for a guy

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a man in the US capital as a waste of space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Washington' just flags an American word for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: A dud is something that fails to work, and the word is used adjectivally for a failed or worthless thing.

clue.text: Making excuses for party involved in cheating

indicators.note: involved in means caught up inside something, so one piece goes within the other

explanation.surface: Someone defends a political party mixed up in fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: To condone is to overlook or excuse wrongdoing, so the participle means forgiving or making allowances for it.

clue.text: Feeble types ultimately shed tears

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very last letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Weaklings end up crying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tears' reads as crying but is the verb pronounced to rhyme with 'bears'.
explanation.definitionFit: Drips is informal slang for weak, insipid, spineless people.

clue.text: Scholars of retail worked to bring in computers

indicators.note: bringing something in puts it inside, so one piece is placed within the other
worked means shaped or kneaded, so the letters are reformed

explanation.surface: Academics studying the shop trade put computers to work.
explanation.definitionFit: Literati are well-read, learned people, educated intellectuals; the plural matches 'scholars'.

clue.text: Abused after admitting one's crooked

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so one piece is let inside the other

parts.note: maligned means spoken ill of, abused
one is I, and 's is is

explanation.surface: Someone vilified finally confesses to being a crook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crooked' suggests dishonesty, but here it just means out of line.
explanation.definitionFit: Something misaligned is set at a wrong angle, askew or out of true, which is crooked in its physical sense.

clue.text: One lover holds back, being inexperienced

indicators.note: back tells us the word runs in the opposite direction
something that holds another keeps it inside itself

parts.note: a fan is a devotee or lover of something

explanation.surface: A shy lover is reticent through lack of experience.
explanation.definitionFit: Naif is a variant of naive, describing someone innocent, unworldly and lacking sophistication.

clue.text: Loom almost covered by blue-green cloth

indicators.note: covered by means wrapped inside something else
almost means not quite the whole word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: to loom is to tower over

explanation.surface: A weaving loom is draped with fabric of a blue-green colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loom' looks like the weaving machine but is the verb meaning to rise menacingly.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea towel is a kitchen cloth used for drying dishes, so the generic word covers it.

clue.text: Pickle got into by Penny's husband

indicators.note: got into by means one thing enters the other, so it ends up inside

parts.note: to souse is to pickle or steep in brine
p is the abbreviation for a penny

explanation.surface: A woman named Penny has a husband who has landed in a fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pickle' reads as a predicament, and Penny as a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A spouse is a marriage partner, and a husband is one example of that relation.

clue.text: Drink with date in sports venue

parts.note: squash is a fruit cordial diluted with water, a common British drink
to court is to woo or go out with someone

explanation.surface: A couple share a drink on a date at a stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain squash is a sweet fruit concentrate topped up with water.
explanation.definitionFit: A squash court is the walled indoor room where the racket game of squash is played, a specific kind of sporting facility.

clue.text: When retired, go crazy!

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn or drawn back, so the word is taken backwards

parts.note: a go or attempt is a stab

explanation.surface: A pensioner is told to go wild once they stop working.
explanation.definitionFit: Bats is informal for mad or eccentric, from having bats in the belfry.

clue.text: Errors introducing attendant delays

indicators.note: introducing means bringing something in, so one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: a page is a young attendant

explanation.surface: An assistant's mistakes cause hold-ups.
explanation.definitionFit: Slippages are failures to keep to schedule, the amount by which a project runs late.

clue.text: It's a nut; he's ebullient

indicators.note: ebullient means bubbling over, so the letters boil up into a new order

explanation.surface: A description of an excitable fanatic.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer too: a nut is a keen fan, and such a fan is ebullient.
explanation.definitionFit: An enthusiast is a keen fan, commonly called a nut, and such devotees are typically bubbling with excitement.

clue.text: Where coal is kept in sinks

definitions.meaning: first meaning: metal buckets for fireside coal
second meaning: deliberately sends a ship to the bottom

explanation.surface: Coal is stored in kitchen sinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinks' looks like the kitchen basins, but it is the verb for sinking a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Coal buckets by a hearth are called by this name, and the same word as a verb means holing a ship deliberately.

clue.text: Sixties icon goes around in skimpy gear

parts.note: the Mini, the small British car launched in 1959, was a 1960s icon
to skirt is to go around the edge of something

explanation.surface: A sixties celebrity tours about in revealing clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Miniskirts are very short skirts, clothing that leaves much uncovered, hence skimpy garments.

clue.text: Withdraw US president's upsetting tweet at last

indicators.note: upsetting means overturning, knocking the letters into a new arrangement

parts.note: Jimmy Carter was a US president

indicators.note: at last points to the very end letter of the word before

explanation.surface: A president is told to take back an offensive social-media post.
explanation.definitionFit: To retract is to take back a statement or pull something in, the same verb sense as withdraw.

clue.text: Complaint received about university

indicators.note: about means going around something, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A grievance about a college has come in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' suggests a grumble, but here it is an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Gout is a painful inflammation of the joints, and complaint is used for any ailment or disorder.

clue.text: Top worn by politician, one that's transparent

indicators.note: what is worn by someone sits over them, so it wraps around the following pieces

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician wears a see-through top.
explanation.definitionFit: Limpid describes water or glass that is perfectly clear, letting light through, a synonym for see-through.

clue.text: A classic artist keeps one uplifted

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted up means read from the bottom upwards
keeps means holds inside, so one piece sits within the other

explanation.surface: A painter keeps one work on a raised display.
explanation.walkthrough: The surrealist holds the numeral, giving DA-I-LI, which is then turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iliad is Homer's Greek epic of the Trojan War, a classic work of literature.

clue.text: Gallery icon is sculpted in rock

indicators.note: sculpted means carved and shaped, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: the Tate is a London art gallery

explanation.surface: A gallery's prized icon is carved from stone.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is a group of major British art galleries.
explanation.definitionFit: Taconite is a hard, low-grade iron ore stone mined chiefly around Lake Superior.

clue.text: Explosive squaddies can set up

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Soldiers are able to rig a bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: A squaddie is British slang for a private soldier; 'can' looks like a verb but is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitro is short for nitroglycerine, the volatile liquid used in dynamite.

clue.text: Man that's checked stock in grocery stores

indicators.note: stores means keeps inside, so the words hold the solution within them

parts.note: hidden across the end of stock, in, and the start of grocery

explanation.surface: A shop worker has done a stock-take in the supermarket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Checked stock' looks like a stocktake; the definition stops at 'checked'.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the pieces are called men, and the most important piece is the one placed in check by the opponent.

clue.text: Acts collecting film Oscars, perhaps

indicators.note: collecting means gathering in, so one piece is taken inside the other

explanation.surface: Performers pick up film awards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acts' suggests stage performers, but it means laws.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oscar is a small gold figurine, so Academy Awards are examples of little sculptures, hence the 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Haggard work has such predictable endings

indicators.note: endings points to the last letter of each word in turn

parts.note: the last letters of has, such and predictable

explanation.surface: A literary critic says a Haggard novel has a formulaic plot.
explanation.walkthrough: H. Rider Haggard was a Victorian adventure novelist; 'haggard' looks like the adjective for worn out.
explanation.definitionFit: H. Rider Haggard's best-known novel, about an immortal queen, is titled with this pronoun, so it is one of his works.

clue.text: An editor sits shuffling paper

indicators.note: shuffling mixes things like cards, so the letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: An editor sits rifling through papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper' tempts as a newspaper the editor runs; it is an academic essay.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissertation is a long academic essay, and paper is used for a scholarly written treatise.
